title: Whether the Ubiquitarians' arguments drawn from the personal union are valid
pass_a_gloss: Article XI. Whether Ubiquitarian arguments from personal union are valid. Para1 First objection of those who invent an immensity of Christ's human nature: whatever is personally joined to the whole Logos exists wherever the Logos exists; Christ's human nature is such; therefore. Reply: major openly false — personal union no more yields humanity everywhere Deity is than substantial union of soul with head-matter yields head-matter wherever soul is (i.e. in the foot). Reductio syllogism for Ubiquists: what is substantially joined to whole soul exists wherever soul exists; head-matter is so joined; soul is in foot-matter; therefore head-matter is in foot-matter. Para2 Second obj: union of two natures in Christ made indivisibly and without interval; therefore one does not exist except where the other does; they coexist in all places. Reply: adverbs inseparably/indistantly have two uses — (1) refute Nestorius who divided natures into two hypostases; (2) teach the union is indissoluble. Deny the consequence that wherever one nature exists the other must; local-presence distinction does not dissolve the union but asserts natures' truth and removes confusion. Para3 First instance: if one nature exists where the other does not, they are separated. Deny connection — soul whole in head-matter is also whole in other members without dissolving union (only death separates). Second instance: soul whole in and outside head-matter is not united by adequate complete union to the head but to partial incomplete matter; by Calvinist view whole Deity in and outside humanity → Logos-humanity union inadequate. Reply: unequal reason — soul/head incomplete because not whole-with-whole (form with whole matter); Logos-humanity is whole-with-whole (whole Deity of Christ with whole humanity in one hypostasis). True reason of inadequacy is not soul outside head-matter but lack of whole-with-whole. So Ubiquitarians wrongly accuse us of dissolving Christ's person; rather we marvel such feeble arguments pleased learned men. Para4 Third obj (Philip Nicolai): Second Person after assuming human nature is always and everywhere DEUS INCARNATUS; therefore nowhere EXCARNATUS. Reply: admit whole argument — excarnation would mean depositing/deserting assumed flesh and dissolving the union; God forbid we say the blessed Logos anywhere strips the Virgin-assumed flesh from his hypostasis. Instance: if Logos exists extra carnem he is somewhere excarnatus. Deny — as whole soul exists outside head-matter with union saved, so whole Logos exists in and outside flesh with personal union saved. Matthias Martinius vs Balthasar Mentzer: extra ambiguous — (a) ultra/beyond (deny inclusion) vs (b) separation (deny union); Logos extra carnem in first sense only. Para5 Second instance: if Logos extra humanitatem in first sense, somewhere not man; but Logos nowhere is not man (always Theanthropos); therefore nowhere extra. Reply: though Aquinas and nearly all scholastics call 'Logos everywhere is man' simply false, distinguish: (A) Logos everywhere is a person having human nature united to him — true, admitted; (B) person having human nature united everywhere and locally present everywhere — plainly false, never admitted. Husband/wife and master/servant analogies show the huge difference. Para6 Third instance: if Logos lacks human nature united and locally coexisting everywhere, whole Christ is not everywhere but only Deity — absurd. Deny connection: from antecedent follows well that totum Christi (all parts) is not everywhere, not that totus Christus is not. Astonished Jacob Andreae and Ubiquitarians reject totus/totum: whole Christ is man but not the whole of Christ; whole Christ suffered/died/rose but not the whole of Christ (both natures). Para7 Fourth instance: Christ is not whole without humanity; so if whole Christ everywhere, humanity everywhere. Deny sequel as ridiculous — parallel: whole Christ not without Deity, so if whole Christ suffered Deity suffered; Christ not whole without his foot, so if whole Christ is man his foot is a man.
pass_b_english: Article XI. Whether the Ubiquitarians' arguments drawn from the personal union are valid.

1. The first objection of those who invent a certain immensity of Christ's human nature is customarily put thus: Whatever is personally joined to the whole Logos exists wherever the Logos exists; but Christ's human nature is such: therefore. The answer is that the proposition is openly false; for from the personal union of the two natures in Christ it no more follows that the humanity is wherever the Deity is, than from the substantial union of our soul with the matter of the head it follows that the matter of the head is wherever the soul is — that is, that it is in the foot, because the soul is in the foot: I say that it is substantially joined to the whole soul, because the whole soul is in the whole body, and whole in each of its parts. If therefore the Ubiquists argue well and acutely when they construct such a syllogism, this argumentation will be good and effective: What is substantially joined to the whole soul exists wherever the soul exists; but the matter of the head is substantially joined to the whole soul: therefore it is wherever the soul is; but the soul is in the matter of the foot; therefore the matter of the head also is in the matter of the foot.

2. Second objection. The union of the two natures in Christ was made indivisibly and without interval: therefore one of them does not exist except where the other exists — that is, they coexist in all places. Answer: the adverbs 'inseparably' and 'indistantly', when used to explain the manner in which those natures are united in the person of the Logos, have a twofold use. First they are used to refute Nestorius's error, who not only distinguished these natures but divided and separated them, assigning to each nature its own proper hypostasis, and therefore did not join them into one hypostasis. Second, that we may know that that union is indissoluble, and that these natures, once they have been joined, can never be disjoined or separated. We therefore deny that consequence: the human and divine natures are indissolubly and inseparably joined in one person; therefore wherever one of them exists, there the other also exists. The reason is that by the distinction of the local presence of the two natures their union is not dissolved, but rather the truth of the natures is asserted and confusion is removed.

3. Someone will press first: If one of those natures exists there where the other does not exist, then one of them is separated from the other; but the former is true: therefore the latter also. Answer by denying the connection: for the human soul, which is whole in the matter of the head, is also whole in the other members in which the matter of the head does not exist; yet the union of the soul with the matter of the head is not by this means dissolved: for, as all know, the soul is torn away and separated from the head and the remaining members only by the death of the human being. Second instance: The soul, which exists whole in the matter of the head and whole outside it, is not united to the head by an adequate and complete union, but is united to it as to a partial and incomplete matter; whereas by an adequate and complete union it is united to the whole body, because the soul is so whole in the whole body that in no way is it outside it. Therefore, since on the Calvinists' view the whole Deity exists in the humanity and also whole outside it, the union of the Logos with the humanity will not be adequate and complete. Answer: the reason is unequal. For the union of the soul with the matter of the head is called incomplete because it is not a union of whole with whole — that is, of the whole form with the whole matter, but with a part of it; but the union of the Logos with the human nature is of whole with whole — that is, of the whole Deity of Christ with his whole humanity, in one hypostasis. The true reason, therefore, why the union of the soul with the matter of the head is inadequate is not that the soul exists outside the matter of the head, but that it is not a union of whole with whole — that is, of the integral form with the integral matter. Wherefore it is not that the Ubiquitarians should object against us that we dissolve the person of Christ, tear apart his natures, and invent an inadequate conjunction of natures for him; on the contrary, we grieve and marvel that such feeble arguments, such childish absurdities, could please and impose upon men distinguished for learning.

4. Third objection. The second person of the Trinity, after he assumed human nature, is always and everywhere GOD INCARNATE: therefore he is nowhere UN-INCARNATE, as Philip Nicolai insolently speaks. Answer: that argument concludes nothing against us, and therefore the whole of it can be admitted. For since the incarnation of God, once posited, consists in the assumption of human nature and its hypostatic conjunction with the divine, it is necessary that 'excarnation' (to speak with Philip Nicolai) signify the depositing, deserting, and dissolving of the union already made: but far be it from us to say that the most blessed Logos anywhere deposits, strips off, or expels from his hypostasis the flesh which he assumed in the Virgin's womb. Someone will press first: if the Logos exists outside the flesh, then he is somewhere un-incarnate; but the former is true on your view; therefore you are bound to admit the latter also. Answer by denying that connection; for just as the whole human soul exists outside the matter of the head with its union to the matter of the head preserved, so also the whole Logos exists both in the flesh and outside the flesh with his personal union to the human nature preserved; and therefore 'to be outside the flesh' does not necessarily infer excarnation, or the dissolution of that personal union. Matthias Martinius, a most acute theologian, answering an argument of this kind proposed by Balthasar Mentzer, says that the little word 'outside' is ambiguous; and that sometimes it is equivalent to 'beyond' — that is, it denies the inclusion of one thing in another; but sometimes it imports separation and denies union. In the former way he says the Logos exists outside the flesh assumed by him, but not in the latter way.

5. Someone will press second: If the Logos, in the former way, is outside the humanity, then somewhere he will not be man; but the Logos is nowhere not man: therefore he is nowhere outside the humanity. The assumption is proved: the Logos is always and everywhere man, for he is always and everywhere the God-man. Answer: Although Saint Thomas, and with him nearly all the scholastic theologians, think that proposition 'the Logos is everywhere man' simply false, yet I judge that a distinction is to be applied. For either this is its sense: the Logos everywhere is a person having human nature united to himself; or this is its sense: the Logos is a person having human nature united to himself everywhere, and therefore locally present to himself everywhere. In the former sense the proposition is true and is admitted by us, because it does not contradict our position; but in the latter it is plainly false, and therefore is never admitted by us. That there is a huge difference between these two senses of that proposition is clear from these examples: 'A husband everywhere, or wherever he exists, is a man having a wife' is a true proposition; but this, 'a husband is everywhere, or in all places, having a wife', is a false proposition. Likewise this, 'A master everywhere is a man having a servant', is a true proposition; but this, 'A master is a man, everywhere having a servant'.

6. Someone will press third: If the Logos does not have human nature united to himself everywhere and locally coexisting, then whole Christ is not everywhere, but only one of his natures, namely the Deity; but the latter is absurd: therefore the former also. Answer by denying the connection of the proposition; for from the antecedent of that connected proposition it follows well that the whole of Christ — that is, all the parts of Christ — is not everywhere; but it does not follow well that whole Christ is not everywhere. Why Doctor Jacob Andreae, and with him the remaining Ubiquitarians, should repudiate this distinction, I greatly wonder. For whole Christ is man, but not the whole of Christ; whole Christ suffered, died, and rose again; but not the whole of Christ — that is, both of his natures.

7. Someone will press fourth: Christ is not whole without the humanity: therefore if whole Christ is everywhere, the humanity of Christ is everywhere. Answer by denying the sequel; for the consequence of that argument is plainly ridiculous and unworthy of refutation, as is clear from these examples which contain a like consequence: Whole Christ is not without the Deity: therefore if whole Christ suffered and died, the Deity also suffered and died. Likewise, Christ is not whole without his foot: therefore if whole Christ is a man, the foot of Christ is a man.
source_text:
ART. XI.
An Ubiquitariorum argumenta ab unione personali petita sint valida.

1. Prima objectio eorum, qui humanae CHRISTI naturae, immensitatem quandam affingunt, sic proponi solet: Quicquid personaliter conjunctum est cum toto Λόγῳ, illud existit ubicunque existit ὁ Λόγος: at natura humana CHRISTI est talis: Ergo. Respondetur, propositionem esse aperte falsam; nam ex personali unione duarum naturarum in CHRISTO, non magis sequitur, humanitatem esse ubicunque est Deitas, quam ex unione substantiali animae nostrae cum materia capitis, sequitur capitis materiam esse ubicunque est anima, h. e. esse in pede, quia anima est in pede: dico eam esse substantialiter conjunctam toti animae, quia tota anima est in toto corpore, & tota in qualibet ejus parte. Si igitur bene & acute argumentantur Ubiquistae, cum talem syllogismum extruunt, bona & efficax erit haec argumentatio: Quod substantialiter est conjunctum toti animae, illud existit ubicunque existit anima: at materia capitis est substantialiter conjuncta toti animae: Ergo est ubicunque est anima: anima autem est in materia pedis, Ergo etiam materia capitis est in materia pedis.

2. Secunda ob. Unio duarum naturarum in CHRISTO facta est ἀδιαιρέτως καὶ ἀδιαστάτως: Ergo non existit earum una nisi ubi existit altera: i. e. in omnibus locis coexistant. Respond. adverbia inseparabiliter & indistanter, cum adhibentur ad explicandum modum, quo uniuntur quae naturae in persona Λόγου, duplicem usum habere: primo enim adhibentur, ad refellendum Nestorii errorem, qui has naturas non tantum distinxit, sed divisit & separavit, utrique naturae suam propriam hypostasin assignans: ideoque illis non conjunxit in unam hypostasin. Secundo, ut sciamus istam unionem esse indissolubilem, & has naturas, postquam semel conjunctae sunt, nunquam disjungi aut separari posse. Negamus igitur istam consequentiam, humana & divina natura indissolubiliter, & inseparabiliter, in una persona conjunctae sunt: Ergo ubicunque existit earum una, ibi etiam existit altera; ratio est, quia per distinctionem localis praesentiae duarum naturarum earum unio non dissolvitur, sed potius naturarum veritas asseritur, & confusio tollitur.

3. Instabit aliquis primo: Si istarum naturarum una ibi existit, ubi non existit altera, tum earum una ab altera separatur: at verum est prius: Ergo etiam posterius. Resp. Negando connexionem: anima enim humana, quae tota est in materia capitis, est etiam tota in aliis membris, in quibus materia capitis non existit; at unio animae cum materia capitis, hoc pacto non dissolvitur: nam, ut omnes norunt, anima non nisi per mortem hominis, divellitur, & separatur a capite, & reliquis membris. Secundo inst. Anima, quae tota existit in materia capitis, & tota extra eam, non unitur capiti unione adaequata & completa; sed ei unitur, tanquam materiae partiali & incompletae: contra vero unione adaequata, et completa unitur toti corpori, quia anima ita est tota in toto corpore, ut nullo modo sit extra illud: Ergo, cum ex sententia Calvinistarum, tota Deitas existat in humanitate, & etiam tota extra eam, unio Του Λόγου cum humanitate, non erit adaequata, & completa. Respond. Imparem esse rationem: unio enim animae cum materia capitis, dicitur incompleta, quia non est unio totius cum toto: i. e. totius formae cum tota materia, sed cum ejus parte: at unio Του Λόγου cum humana natura, est totius cum toto: i. e. totius Deitatis CHRISTI, cum tota ejus humanitate, in una hypostasi. Vera igitur ratio cur unio animae cum materia capitis, sit inadaequata, non est quod anima existat extra materiam capitis, sed quod non sit unio totius cum toto: i. e. integrae formae cum integra materia. Quamobrem non est, quod Ubiquitarii nobis objiciant, nos personam CHRISTI solvere, naturas ipsius divellere, & inadaequatam conjunctionem naturarum ei affingere: sed contra est quod nos doleamus, & miremur, tam exilia argumenta, tam pueriles ineptias, viris ab eruditione claris placere, & imponere potuisse.

4. Tertia ob. Secunda persona Trinitatis, postquam humanam naturam assumpsit, semper & ubique est DEUS INCARNATUS: Ergo nusquam est EXCARNATUS, ut insolenter loquitur Philippus Nicolai. Resp. Illud argumentum, nihil concludere contra nos, & proinde totum admitti posse: cum enim incarnatio DEI posita, sit in humanae naturae assumptione, ejusque conjunctione hypostatica cum divina, necesse est excarnationem (ut cum Philippo Nicolai loquar) significare humanae naturae depositionem, desertionem, & unionis jam factae dissolutionem: absit autem dicamus beatissimum Λόγον carnem, quam in utero Virginis assumpsit, alicubi deponere, exuere, aut e sua hypostasi exterminare. Instabit aliquis primo: si ὁ Λόγος existit extra carnem, ergo est alicubi excarnatus: at verum est prius, ex vestra sententia. Ergo etiam posterius admittere tenemini. Resp. Negando illam connexionem; sicut enim tota anima humana, existit extra materiam capitis, salva ejus unione cum materia capitis, ita etiam totus Λόγος existit & in carne, & extra carnem, salva sua personali unione cum natura humana; & proinde τὸ esse extra carnem non necessario infert excarnationem, seu unionis istius personalis dissolutionem. Matthias Martinius acutissimus Theologus, ad hujusmodi argumentum a Balthasare Mentzero propositum respondens, dicit voculam extra esse ambiguam; & alias idem valere quod ultra, h. e. negare rei unius inclusionem in alia re: alias autem, importare separationem, & negare unionem; priore modo dicit τὸν Λόγον existere extra carnem a se assumptam, non vero posteriore modo.

5. Instabit aliquis secundo: Si Λόγος, priori modo est extra humanitatem, ergo alicubi non erit homo: at Λόγος nusquam non est homo: Ergo nusquam est extra humanitatem: probatur assumptio: Λόγος semper & ubique est homo nam semper & ubique est Θεάνθρωπος. Resp. Quamvis Sanctus Thomas, & cum eo fere omnes Scholastici Theologi, putent illam propositionem, Λόγος ubique est homo, simpliciter esse falsam, puto tamen distinctionem esse adhibendam: vel enim hic est ejus sensus, Λόγος ubique est persona, humanam naturam sibi unitam habens: vel hic est ejus sensus, Λόγος est persona habens naturam humanam, ubique sibi unitam, ideoque ubique sibi localiter praesentem. In priori sensu propositio est vera, & a nobis admittitur; quia nostrae sententiae non contradicit: in posteriore vero, plane falsa est, & proinde a nobis nunquam admittitur. Inter hos duos sensus istius propositionis, ingens esse discrimen, ex his exemplis liquet: Maritus ubique, seu ubicunque existit, est vir uxorem habens, est propositio vera: at haec, maritus est ubique, seu in omnibus locis uxorem habens, est propositio falsa: Similiter haec, Dominus ubique est vir, servum habens, propositio est vera: haec vero, Dominus est vir, ubique servum habens.

6. Instabit aliquis tertio: Si ὁ Λόγος non habet naturam humanam ubique sibi unitam & localiter coexistentem, totus Christus non est ubique, sed una tantum ejus natura, videlicet Deitas: at absurdum est posterius, Ergo etiam prius. Resp. Negando connexionem propositionis, nam ex antecedente istius connexae propositionis, bene sequitur totum CHRISTI, i. e. omnes partes CHRISTI, non esse ubique; non vero bene sequitur totum CHRISTUM non esse ubique. Hanc distinctionem cur repudiet D. Jacobus Andreae, & cum eo reliqui Ubiquitarii, magnopere demiror: Totus enim CHRISTUS est homo, sed non totum CHRISTI; totus CHRISTUS est passus, mortuus, & resurrexit; sed non totum CHRISTI: i. e. utraque ejus natura.

7. Instabit aliquis quarto: CHRISTUS non est totus, sine humanitate: Ergo si totus CHRISTUS est ubique, humanitas CHRISTI est ubique. Resp. Negando sequelam; istius enim argumenti consequentia, est plane ridicula, & refutatione indigna, ut patet ex his exemplis, quae similem consequentiam continent: Totus CHRISTUS non est sine Deitate: Ergo si totus CHRISTUS est passus & mortuus, Deitas etiam passa est, & mortua: Item, CHRISTUS non est totus, sine pede suo: Ergo si totus CHRISTUS est homo, pes CHRISTI est homo.
